questions.stem: What is a unicellular organism?
options: An organism made of many identical cells that each live independently
An organism made of specialised cells organised into tissues and organs
An organism made of one type of tissue that forms a single organ
An organism made of a single cell that carries out all life processes
questions.explanation: A unicellular organism, such as a bacterium, Amoeba or Paramecium, is one cell that must feed, respire, excrete, respond and reproduce on its own. Specialised cells in tissues and organs describe a multicellular organism.

questions.stem: Which organism is a colonial organism?
options: Amoeba, a protist
A eucalyptus tree
A soil bacterium cell
Volvox, a green alga
questions.explanation: Volvox forms hollow spheres of many similar flagellated cells joined together. Amoeba and bacteria are unicellular, and a eucalyptus is a multicellular plant with tissues and organs.

questions.stem: Paramecium lives in fresh water and has contractile vacuoles that fill and empty regularly. What is their function?
options: Expelling the excess water that keeps entering the cell by osmosis
Digesting food particles that the cell has taken in from the water
Storing starch made by photosynthesis for use when light is scarce
Moving the cell through the water by squirting jets from its surface
questions.explanation: Fresh water is hypotonic to the cytoplasm, so water constantly enters by osmosis; contractile vacuoles collect and pump it out so the cell does not burst. Digestion happens in separate food vacuoles, and Paramecium moves using cilia.

questions.stem: How does an Amoeba obtain food, as a single cell with no mouth or gut?
options: It absorbs light through chloroplasts and makes glucose by photosynthesis
It takes in large food particles by simple diffusion straight through its membrane
It relies on other cells in its colony to digest food and pass it on
It extends pseudopodia around food particles and takes them in by phagocytosis
questions.explanation: Amoeba surrounds food with cytoplasmic extensions and encloses it in a food vacuole, where enzymes digest it. It has no chloroplasts, large particles cannot diffuse through the membrane, and it is not colonial.

questions.stem: Euglena has chloroplasts, a flagellum and a light-sensitive eyespot. How do these structures work together?
options: The chloroplasts detect light, and the eyespot digests food that the flagellum sweeps into the cell
The eyespot absorbs carbon dioxide, and the flagellum releases the oxygen made by the chloroplasts
The eyespot detects light, and the flagellum moves the cell towards it so the chloroplasts can photosynthesise
The flagellum makes glucose, and the eyespot stores it until the chloroplasts need the energy for movement
questions.explanation: In a single cell, different organelles carry out different functions: sensing light, moving and photosynthesising. Together they let Euglena position itself where it can make food.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a colonial organism from a multicellular organism?
options: Colonial organisms are made of prokaryotic cells; multicellular organisms are always made of plant cells
Colonial organisms have only one cell; multicellular organisms have two or more cells joined by membranes
Colonial cells are similar and only slightly specialised; multicellular cells are highly specialised and interdependent
Colonial cells are highly specialised into tissues; multicellular cells are identical and each lives independently
questions.explanation: In a colony, cells are mostly alike and cooperate, with limited division of labour. In a multicellular organism, cells differentiate into specialised types that depend on one another and cannot survive alone.

questions.stem: The cells of a Volvox colony each have two flagella. How does the colony move towards light?
options: The flagella of the cells beat in a coordinated way, rolling the whole colony along
Each cell detaches and swims separately, and the cells rejoin when they reach the light
The colony fills with gas produced by photosynthesis and floats up towards the light
Specialised muscle cells inside the sphere contract and push the colony forwards
questions.explanation: Cells in the colony are linked by cytoplasmic strands and coordinate their flagella, so the colony behaves as one unit. Volvox has no muscle tissue.

questions.stem: In Volvox, most cells cannot reproduce, while a few larger cells produce new colonies. What does this suggest about colonial organisms?
options: Colonies reproduce only sexually, because the larger cells must be gametes from other colonies
Colonies can show a simple division of labour, a step between unicellular and multicellular life
Colonies are fully multicellular, because every one of their cells is specialised into tissues and organs
Colonies are unicellular, because every cell in the colony can survive and reproduce alone
questions.explanation: Having some cells specialised for reproduction is a limited form of specialisation, more than in a loose group of identical cells but far less than in organisms with tissues and organs. This makes Volvox a useful model of how multicellularity may have evolved.

questions.stem: What is an advantage of being multicellular rather than unicellular?
options: The organism can reproduce by binary fission, so populations grow very quickly
Specialised cells can each perform one function efficiently, allowing larger size
Every cell is in direct contact with the environment, so no transport system is needed
Each cell can survive on its own if it becomes separated from the organism
questions.explanation: Division of labour among differentiated cells allows complex functions and large body size. Most cells in a large organism are not in contact with the environment, which is why transport systems are needed.

questions.stem: Why do large multicellular animals need transport and exchange systems?
options: Their cells are much larger than unicellular organisms, so each one needs more nutrients
Their cells cannot carry out respiration, so energy must be delivered to them as ATP
Their body surface is impermeable, so no substances can diffuse across it at all
Most of their cells are too far from the body surface for diffusion alone to supply them
questions.explanation: Diffusion is only fast over very short distances. In a large body, inner cells are far from the surface and the overall SA:V ratio is low, so lungs, gut and a circulatory system are needed. Body cells are generally similar in size to single-celled organisms.

questions.stem: What is cell differentiation?
options: The process by which a cell divides to form two genetically different daughter cells
The process by which cells of different species fuse together to form a colony
The process by which a cell loses its nucleus before it becomes a gamete
The process by which unspecialised cells become specialised for particular functions
questions.explanation: During development, cells switch particular genes on and off and become specialised, such as nerve, muscle or xylem cells. Differentiation does not involve division into genetically different cells.

questions.stem: A Paramecium cell and a human muscle cell both respire, but only the Paramecium also feeds, osmoregulates, moves and reproduces by itself. What best explains this difference?
options: The muscle cell is specialised and relies on other cells and systems for its other needs
The muscle cell contains no mitochondria, so it depends on blood for its supply of ATP
The Paramecium is a multicellular organism made of many cells with different functions
The Paramecium has a much higher volume than the muscle cell, so it needs more organelles
questions.explanation: A unicellular organism must perform every life function within one cell. A specialised cell in a multicellular body performs one main role and depends on digestive, circulatory and excretory systems for the rest. Muscle cells contain many mitochondria.

questions.stem: Why is the surface-area-to-volume ratio of a cell important?
options: The volume is where materials are exchanged, while the surface determines how much the cell needs
A high ratio means the cell is too large to divide, so it must stay the same size
A low ratio allows materials to diffuse into the cell faster than a high ratio does
The surface is where materials are exchanged, while the volume determines how much the cell needs
questions.explanation: All substances enter and leave through the membrane, and the cytoplasm's volume sets the demand. A higher SA:V ratio gives more surface per unit of volume, so exchange can keep up with demand.

questions.stem: An agar block is a cube 3 cm along each side. What is its surface-area-to-volume ratio?
questions.explanation: Surface area = 6 × 3² = 54 cm² and volume = 3³ = 27 cm³, so the ratio is 54 : 27 = 2 : 1. A 1 cm cube would have a ratio of 6 : 1.

questions.stem: A cube-shaped cell doubles the length of each side. What happens to its surface-area-to-volume ratio?
options: It halves
It doubles
It stays the same
It quarters
questions.explanation: Surface area increases by 2² = 4 times but volume by 2³ = 8 times, so the ratio becomes 4/8 = 1/2 of its original value. For a cube, SA:V = 6 ÷ side length.

questions.stem: A cube-shaped cell has sides of 10 µm. What is its surface-area-to-volume ratio?
questions.explanation: Surface area = 6 × 10² = 600 µm² and volume = 10³ = 1000 µm³, giving 600 : 1000 = 0.6 : 1. Inverting the ratio gives about 1.7, which is volume to surface area.

questions.stem: A block of agar measures 1 cm × 1 cm × 4 cm. A cube of agar with the same volume has sides of about 1.6 cm and a SA:V ratio of about 3.8 : 1. What is the SA:V ratio of the long block, and what does the comparison show?
options: 18 : 1; a long, thin shape has a much higher ratio than any cube can have
4.5 : 1; a long, thin shape has a higher ratio than a cube of the same volume
4.5 : 1; a long, thin shape has a lower ratio than a cube of the same volume
2.3 : 1; a long, thin shape has a lower ratio than a cube of the same volume
questions.explanation: Surface area = 2(1×1 + 1×4 + 1×4) = 18 cm² and volume = 4 cm³, so SA:V = 4.5 : 1, higher than the cube's 3.8 : 1. Flattened or elongated shapes, like nerve cells and leaves, increase SA:V without reducing volume.

questions.stem: Why are most cells very small?
options: A small cell has a high SA:V ratio, so diffusion can supply all of its cytoplasm quickly
A small cell has a low SA:V ratio, so it loses fewer useful substances to its surroundings
A small cell has less DNA, so it can divide more often than a large cell can
A small cell needs no membrane proteins, because everything diffuses through the bilayer
questions.explanation: As a cell grows, its volume rises faster than its surface area, so exchange across the membrane eventually cannot meet the cell's needs, and the centre is far from the surface. Dividing keeps cells small with a high SA:V.

questions.stem: Agar cubes containing a pink indicator are placed in acid, which turns the agar colourless as it diffuses in. In this experiment, what is the independent variable?
options: The time left in the acid
The colour of the indicator
The size of the agar cubes
The concentration of the acid
questions.explanation: The investigation tests how cube size, and so SA:V ratio, affects how much of the cube the acid reaches. Acid concentration and time are controlled variables, and the colour change is how the dependent variable is observed.

questions.stem: In the agar cube experiment, acid diffuses 0.25 cm into every face of a 2 cm cube. What percentage of the cube's volume has turned colourless?
options: About 88%
About 58%
About 25%
About 42%
questions.explanation: The unchanged centre is a cube of side 2 − 0.5 = 1.5 cm, with volume 3.375 cm³ out of 8 cm³ (about 42%). So about 100 − 42 = 58% has changed. About 88% would be the figure for a 1 cm cube.

questions.stem: In the agar experiment, acid penetrated the same depth into 1 cm, 2 cm and 4 cm cubes, but changed about 88%, 58% and 33% of their volumes. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: As size increases, SA:V increases, so a greater proportion of the volume is reached by diffusion
Cube size has no effect, because the acid travelled the same distance into each of the cubes
As size increases, SA:V decreases, so a smaller proportion of the volume is reached by diffusion
As size increases, diffusion becomes slower, so the acid travels a shorter distance into bigger cubes
questions.explanation: Diffusion rate (depth reached) was the same, but larger cubes have less surface per unit volume, so a smaller fraction of their volume was reached. This models why large cells could not supply their centres by diffusion.

questions.stem: In the agar cube experiment, which variable must be controlled to make the comparison valid?
options: The concentration and temperature of the acid for all cubes
The size of each cube, which must be the same for all of them
The percentage of each cube that turns colourless at the end
The time of day at which each of the different cubes is cut
questions.explanation: Acid concentration, temperature and soaking time all affect diffusion, so they must be kept the same. Cube size is the independent variable and the percentage changed is the dependent variable.

questions.stem: Flatworms have no circulatory system or lungs, yet oxygen reaches all their cells. How?
options: Their skin pumps oxygen in by active transport, using energy released from ATP
Their cells do not respire, so they have no need for oxygen to be supplied
Their flat bodies keep every cell close to the surface, so diffusion is fast enough
Their cells are much larger than other animal cells, so they store extra oxygen
questions.explanation: A flat, thin body gives a large surface area relative to volume and a short diffusion distance to every cell. Thicker animals need specialised gas exchange surfaces and transport systems.

questions.stem: Cells lining the small intestine have microvilli on the surface facing the gut. How do these help the cells?
options: They push food along the intestine by beating in coordinated waves like cilia
They secrete mucus that protects the cells from digestive enzymes
They reduce the volume of each cell so it needs fewer nutrients
They greatly increase the surface area for absorbing digested nutrients
questions.explanation: Microvilli are tiny folds of the cell membrane that multiply the absorptive surface without much increase in volume. Moving material along the gut is done by muscular contractions (peristalsis).

questions.stem: How is a root hair cell adapted for absorbing water and mineral ions?
options: A large number of chloroplasts provides glucose for active uptake of water
A thick wall of lignin gives the cell strength to push through the hard soil
A long, thin extension greatly increases its surface area in contact with soil water
A thick waxy cuticle stops water from leaving the cell again once it has been absorbed
questions.explanation: The hair-like projection increases the cell's surface area and SA:V for osmosis and ion uptake. Root hairs have no chloroplasts, and a waxy cuticle or lignified wall would block absorption.

questions.stem: Mammalian red blood cells are biconcave discs with no nucleus. How does the biconcave shape help their function?
options: It increases the cell's volume, so more glucose can be stored for respiration
It makes the cell rigid, so it cannot be squeezed through narrow capillaries
It increases the SA:V ratio, speeding the diffusion of oxygen in and out
It decreases the SA:V ratio, so oxygen cannot leak out before it is needed
questions.explanation: Thinning the centre of the disc gives a large surface for a small volume and a short diffusion distance to the haemoglobin. Red blood cells are flexible, which lets them fold to pass through capillaries.

questions.stem: A mouse must eat a much larger mass of food relative to its body mass than an elephant. How does SA:V help explain this?
options: The mouse has a lower SA:V ratio, so it gains heat too quickly and wastes energy as sweat
The mouse has a higher SA:V ratio, so it loses body heat faster and must respire more per gram
The mouse has a lower SA:V ratio, so it absorbs food more slowly and must eat more of it
The mouse has a higher SA:V ratio, so it absorbs too much heat and must eat to cool down
questions.explanation: Small animals have a large surface relative to their volume, so heat escapes quickly. To keep its body temperature steady, a mouse must release more heat by respiration per gram of tissue, which needs more food.

questions.stem: How do large organisms overcome their low overall SA:V ratio?
options: With slower metabolism in every cell, so that none of their cells needs any oxygen
With specialised exchange surfaces such as lungs, gills and leaves, plus transport systems
With cells that are much larger than those of small organisms, to store more materials
With a thick, waterproof outer layer that stops all exchange with the environment
questions.explanation: Folded or thin structures such as alveoli, gill filaments, villi and leaves provide a huge surface area, and blood or vascular tissue carries materials to and from every cell. Cell size is broadly similar in small and large organisms.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the levels of organisation in a multicellular organism, from smallest to largest?
options: Organelle, cell, tissue, organ, system
Cell, organelle, tissue, system, organ
Organelle, tissue, cell, organ, system
Tissue, cell, organelle, organ, system
questions.explanation: Organelles make up cells, similar cells form tissues, tissues combine into organs, and organs work together as systems. Organs are part of systems, not the other way round.

questions.stem: What is a tissue?
options: A structure within a cell that carries out a specific job for the cell
A group of different organs working together to carry out a life process
A single specialised cell that can carry out all of the organism's functions
A group of similar cells working together to perform a particular function
questions.explanation: Examples of tissues are muscle tissue, epithelium and xylem. A structure within a cell is an organelle, and a group of organs is a system.

questions.stem: Which part of a flowering plant is an organ?
options: A guard cell
A leaf
A chloroplast
A xylem vessel
questions.explanation: A leaf is made of several tissues, including epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll, xylem and phloem, working together. A chloroplast is an organelle, a guard cell is a cell and xylem is a tissue.

questions.stem: Which list correctly matches cardiac muscle, the heart and the circulatory system to their levels of organisation?
options: Organ, system, tissue
Tissue, system, organ
Tissue, organ, system
Cell, tissue, organ
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is a tissue of similar cells; the heart is an organ containing muscle, connective and nervous tissue; together with blood vessels and blood it forms the circulatory system.

questions.stem: Xylem in a plant stem contains vessel elements, fibres and some living cells, which work together to carry water. At which level of organisation is xylem?
options: Organ
Organelle
System
Tissue
questions.explanation: Xylem is a group of cells working together for one main function, so it is a tissue (a complex tissue with several cell types). The stem that contains it is an organ.

questions.stem: Glucose absorbed in the small intestine reaches muscle cells in the leg. Which systems work together to make this possible?
options: The excretory system and the digestive system
The digestive system and the circulatory system
The respiratory system and the excretory system
The nervous system and the skeletal system
questions.explanation: The digestive system breaks down and absorbs food, and the circulatory system carries the glucose in the blood to body cells. Systems in a multicellular organism depend on each other.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly traces the levels of organisation involved in photosynthesis in a eucalypt?
options: Chloroplast, palisade mesophyll, palisade cell, shoot system, leaf
Leaf, chloroplast, palisade cell, shoot system, palisade mesophyll
Chloroplast, palisade cell, palisade mesophyll, leaf, shoot system
Palisade cell, chloroplast, leaf, palisade mesophyll, shoot system
questions.explanation: The chloroplast (organelle) is inside a palisade cell (cell); many palisade cells form the palisade mesophyll (tissue); tissues form the leaf (organ); leaves, stems and buds make up the shoot system.

questions.stem: At which level of organisation is a mitochondrion?
options: Tissue
Organ
Organelle
Cell
questions.explanation: A mitochondrion is a membrane-bound structure inside a eukaryotic cell, so it is an organelle. Cells contain organelles, not the other way around.
